title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: An outside actor breached North Carolina Ports’ IT systems, forcing all three facilities onto manual cargo processing
items.content_text: The North Carolina State Ports Authority disclosed that an intrusion detected on 5 August compromised IT systems supporting all three of its facilities: the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City, and the Charlotte inland terminal. A spokesperson confirmed the breach was carried out by an outside actor and that cargo processing shifted to manual procedures while the authority worked to contain the incident; the breach was publicly reported on 6 August. The operator declined to say whether ransomware was involved, leaving that question unresolved. The authority described the intrusion as contained, and said normal operating schedules resumed on 6 and 7 August, though some processing remained manual afterward. No group has publicly claimed responsibility. Critically, the authority has not confirmed that any operational technology — crane control systems, terminal operating systems, or gate automation — was compromised, but it has also not explicitly ruled that out; the public statements to date describe an IT-system breach and a manual fallback, not a completed OT forensic finding. That gap matters for the sector: a manual-processing fallback that worked is exactly the kind of contingency capability the Coast Guard’s cybersecurity rule for the Marine Transportation System expects operators to have rehearsed, and this incident is a live test of whether that capability exists industry-wide rather than at one operator. Three facilities running on manual procedures simultaneously for roughly two days also shows how quickly an IT-only breach can visibly affect cargo flow even without any claim of OT manipulation.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina Ports Authority statement — via The Record
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 5 Aug 2026; publicly reported 6 Aug 2026, normal schedules resumed 6–7 Aug

items.title: A CEVA Logistics intrusion halted outbound shipments at eight European warehouses, rippling into retail and gaming supply chains
items.content_text: CEVA Logistics, a contract-logistics and freight-forwarding provider, suffered an intrusion on 29 July that disrupted its European operations and stopped outbound shipments from eight warehouses. The company notified customers on 1 August, and the scale of the disruption became public in the week of 10 August. Air, ocean, ground and rail transport services were not affected — the disruption was confined to warehouse and contract-logistics IT. CEVA says personal data including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and order details was compromised, but that payment and credential data was not. Downstream retailers and brands named as affected include Bol, De Bijenkorf, Ace & Tate, Pokémon Center (UK and Germany, with some order cancellations), Valve/Steam, Ajax and ING; the Dutch data protection authority is investigating. No group has claimed the intrusion. For ports and terminals the relevance is dependency, not direct exposure: contract-logistics and warehousing providers like CEVA sit between ocean carriers, consignees and inland distribution, and an eight-warehouse outage shows how a logistics-IT breach with no port or vessel OT involvement can still back up cargo movement downstream of the berth.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CEVA Logistics customer notifications — via The Record
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 29 Jul 2026; scale publicly reported week of 10 Aug 2026

items.title: Johnson Controls patches critical deserialization flaws that could hand over physical access-control systems
items.content_text: Johnson Controls updated its advisory (Update A, 11 August) for C•CURE 9000 and victor, its physical access-control and video platforms, covering two critical unauthenticated deserialization vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-21655 and CVE-2026-21653) and a high-severity issue (CVE-2026-34496), with CVSS scores up to 9.6. A network-adjacent attacker who reaches the application server can exploit the deserialization flaws without credentials to execute arbitrary code and take control of the access-control system itself. C•CURE and victor deployments commonly manage terminal gate access, badge readers, perimeter doors and camera integrations at ports and other regulated facilities, which is the deployment pattern that makes this advisory relevant here even though it is not marine-specific. No public exploitation has been reported. Patches are available.

items.title: Siemens fixes a critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video that a permissioned user could trigger
items.content_text: Siemens patched CVE-2026-3014, an OS command-injection flaw rated CVSS 9.1, in Siveillance Video management servers as part of the August ICS Patch Tuesday cycle. A user who already holds edit permissions within the video-management system can use the flaw to run arbitrary code on the server. Video-management platforms of this kind are widely used for port and terminal perimeter and yard surveillance, including camera networks tied into gate and access-control operations, so this exposure sits close to the same physical-security stack as the Johnson Controls access-control advisory in this window. A patch is available.

items.title: A Cisco ASA/FTD firewall flaw is being actively exploited to crash devices, with a three-day federal patch deadline
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-20349, a CVSS 8.6 heap-inspection denial-of-service flaw in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Firepower Threat Defense software, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 11 August, with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Cisco has shipped hotfixes across the affected 9.x, 7.x and 10.x branches; there is no workaround. Cisco ASA and FTD appliances are commonly deployed as the boundary device between corporate IT and OT or terminal-operating networks, including remote-access VPNs used by vendors and remote engineers, which makes an availability flaw here an operational risk beyond the firewall itself even though the bug does not grant code execution.

items.title: CISA and international partners warn Gunra ransomware is breaking in through unpatched internet-facing VPN gateways
items.content_text: CISA, the FBI and international partners published joint advisory AA26-222A on 10 August covering Gunra, a Conti-derived ransomware-as-a-service operation running double-extortion attacks against government and critical-infrastructure targets. The advisory says initial access typically comes through unpatched internet-facing VPN gateways and exposed RDP, citing Fortinet flaws CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 specifically, and describes a five-to-seven-day payment deadline once operators gain a foothold. Ports and terminals rely on the same class of equipment — VPN concentrators and remote-access gateways — for vendor, engineering and remote-berth connectivity, which is the entry path this advisory describes rather than any port-specific targeting.

items.title: Siemens patches XSS and path-traversal flaws in the RUGGEDCOM APE1808 substation and remote-site computing platform
items.content_text: Siemens fixed two vulnerabilities in the RUGGEDCOM APE1808 application-hosting platform in the August Patch Tuesday cycle: a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-23573) and a path-traversal issue inherited from bundled Fortinet components (CVE-2026-59839), rated CVSS 6.1 and 5.5. RUGGEDCOM devices are ruggedized computing and networking platforms used at substations and other remote or harsh-environment sites in energy and transportation, including shore-power, substation and remote-site infrastructure serving port facilities. An update is available, and Siemens recommends also applying the relevant Fortinet guidance for the bundled components.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT advisory — via WaterISAC ICS advisory roundup

items.title: Johnson Controls fixes a hardcoded cryptographic key in its Airwall secure remote-access product
items.content_text: Johnson Controls patched two vulnerabilities in Airwall, its OT secure-remote-access product: a hardcoded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-64887, CVSS 6.8) and a path-traversal flaw allowing arbitrary file read (CVE-2026-34492, CVSS 6.4). CISA notes neither is remotely exploitable and both require high attack complexity, and both are fixed in version 4.1.0. Airwall is used to broker remote vendor and engineer access into OT networks — exactly the kind of remote-access path that ports use for crane, reefer and terminal-system vendors, and the same class of connectivity the Gunra advisory in this window flags as a common ransomware entry point when misconfigured or unpatched.

items.title: Dragos counts eight maritime ransomware incidents in Q2, inside a transportation total of 95 — and no direct control-system manipulation
items.content_text: Dragos’s Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis, published 10 August, recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents against industrial organizations worldwide, up 12% on Q1. Within the transportation and logistics category — 95 incidents total — Dragos counted 8 against maritime targets, alongside 6 in aviation and 3 in rail; manufacturing dominated the overall total at 747 of 1,140. The most active groups named were Qilin, Akira, The Gentlemen, DragonForce and LockBit 5.0. Dragos’s key structural finding is that most intrusions cascaded into operational disruption through IT-system encryption rather than direct manipulation of control systems — no Stage 2 ICS Kill Chain activity was observed. North Carolina Ports fits that pattern: an IT breach with real operational consequences at the gate, without any confirmed OT compromise, which is the same mechanism Dragos describes across the wider ransomware count.

items.title: The live water-utility PLC campaign is a warning for any port with an internet-reachable controller
items.content_text: Since late July, actors assessed by CISA, the FBI, NSA and other agencies to be Iranian-affiliated (joint advisory AA26-097A) have reached internet-exposed Rockwell Automation MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers at water utilities in at least 12 states, changing device IP addresses and setting unauthorized passwords to lock operators out — using exposure and weak or default credentials, not a disclosed CVE, to get in. Forescout Vedere Labs separately catalogued 4,407 internet-exposed Rockwell/Allen-Bradley controllers worldwide, 2,844 of them in the US, dominated by discontinued legacy MicroLogix hardware, including 22 units in cities already hit by the attacks. Neither finding is about the marine sector directly, but the mechanism generalizes to any facility running internet-reachable legacy controllers with weak authentication — a description that fits crane, ballast, bilge and gate-automation PLCs at some terminals as much as it fits a water utility’s pump controls. The operative lesson is exposure and credential hygiene, not a patch to apply.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Forescout Vedere Labs research; CISA/FBI/NSA joint advisory AA26-097A — via TechCrunch

items.title: Dragos publishes phased segmentation guidance to help port and vessel operators meet MTSA’s network-separation requirement
items.content_text: Dragos published guidance on 3 August (“Who’s Allowed on the Bridge”) aimed at port and vessel operators working toward the Coast Guard’s Maritime Transportation Security Act cybersecurity requirement for network segmentation. It lays out a phased crawl/walk/run approach: building an enterprise-to-OT DMZ, controlling remote-access brokers, and separating operational wireless and radio links — bridge, crane and shipboard systems among them — from control networks. The guidance targets operators starting from limited or no existing OT security architecture rather than assuming a green-field build.
